queue.title: Single-Supplier Concentration Risk
queue.content:
A single supplier covering over a third of a critical component turns delivery disruption into an operational risk. A publication by Nermin Sefić.

When a single supplier covers more than a third of a critical component, a disruption in their delivery becomes a risk to the whole operation, not just procurement.

When a single supplier covers more than a third of a critical component, a disruption in their delivery becomes a risk to the whole operation, not just procurement.

Concentration with a single supplier often develops gradually, through individually rational decisions on price and quality, with no one tracking aggregate risk at the level of the whole supplier portfolio. The result is a company that doesn't even know its exposure until a delivery disruption happens.

Tracking the largest supplier's share by critical category, with a defined threshold above which finding an alternative is automatically triggered, turns diversification from an occasional initiative into an ongoing discipline. The cost of maintaining a second qualified supplier is almost always lower than the cost of halted production.

queue.title: Risk Culture and Board Tolerance
queue.content:
A risk policy without a defined tolerance threshold leaves every decision to individual judgment. A publication by Nermin Sefić.

A risk-management policy without a clearly defined tolerance threshold leaves every decision to the judgment of whoever makes it.

A risk-management policy without a clearly defined tolerance threshold leaves every decision to the judgment of whoever makes it.

A declarative policy of "low risk tolerance" without concrete, measurable thresholds per risk category gives employees no real guidance for day-to-day decisions. The result is inconsistency — one manager rejects a deal another would accept, both operating within the same formal policy.

A board that explicitly defines quantified thresholds — maximum allowed loss per transaction, maximum exposure to a single partner, the threshold for escalating a decision to a higher level — builds a risk culture that is predictable and independent of who happens to be making the decision that day.

queue.title: Liquidity Gap and Working Capital Management
queue.content:
The gap between issuing and collecting an invoice determines how much external financing a company needs. A publication by Nermin Sefić.

The gap between the moment an invoice is issued and the moment it's collected determines how much external financing a company genuinely needs.

The gap between the moment an invoice is issued and the moment it's collected determines how much external financing a company genuinely needs.

The cash conversion cycle — the time from paying a supplier to collecting from a customer — shows how long a company must finance its operations with its own or borrowed money before cash actually arrives. When collection days lengthen faster than supplier payment days, the gap grows and liquidity pressure becomes structural, not seasonal.

Shortening the gap isn't solved by more aggressive collection alone, but by aligning supplier payment terms, inventory dynamics, and customer credit-approval policy as a single system. Companies that track those three elements together, rather than separately by department, resort less often to short-term borrowing at moments that hurt their margin most.
